entry.title: Lau Lab NAS Standard Operating Procedure

link.title: Lau Lab NAS Standard Operating Procedure

entry.content:
Overview

NAS Capacity Notes
Polaris LauLab 150 TB total 50 TB reserved for Monica; 100 TB open to everyone. Primary storage for all lab data. Mounted on Rosalind at /Polaris/LauLab
Rosalind NAS 100 TB (⚠️ 70% full) Mounted at /home/NAShome. Every user’s home directory is at /home/NAS/VUNetID/
Synology NAS (LauLabNAS1) 62.8 TB usable / 12.7 TB free Access via browser at http://10.18.26.54:5000/. Open to everyone. Only level_1_data is mounted on Rosalind at /mnt/launas

Synology NAS (LauLabNAS1)

⚠️ Note: Synology NAS is a consumer/prosumer-grade system and is slower than Polaris. It is not optimized for heavy computation or large dataset I/O. Use it for storing documents, scripts, and level1_data intake only. For intensive workloads, use Polaris/Rosalind instead.

Storage Info

  Details
RAID type Synology Hybrid RAID (SHR) — 2-drive fault tolerance
Storage Pool Storage Pool 1 — 65.4 TB (6× 16.4 TB HDDs)
SSD Cache RAID 0 — 745 GB (2× 372.6 GB M.2 drives)
Volume 1 62.8 TB total, 12.7 TB free (Btrfs)
Status Healthy ✅

How to Check Available Space

  1. Log in at http://10.18.26.54:5000/
  2. Open Storage Manager from the main menu
  3. In the left sidebar, click Storage Pool 1 or Volume 1
  4. The top of the page shows allocated space and free space at a glance

Accessing via Browser

  1. Connect to VPN
  2. Go to http://10.18.26.54:5000/
  3. Log in with your credentials

Accessing via Your Computer

Windows

  1. Make sure you are on VPN (or connected via ethernet)
  2. Search for “Turn Windows Features on or off”
  3. Find SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support and check the box to enable it, then restart your computer
  4. Open File Explorer, navigate to Network, and right-click to get options
  5. Select Map Network Drive
  6. Choose any drive letter and enter the server path: 
    \\10.18.26.54\<folder_to_mount>
  7. Check “Use different credentials”
  8. Enter your credentials when prompted:
    • Username: LauLabNAS1\<your_username>
    • Password: your NAS account password

Mac

Method 1 — via Notes App

  1. Make sure you are on VPN
  2. Open the Notes application
  3. In a new note, type: smb://username@LauLabNAS1/
  4. A dialog will appear: “You are attempting to connect to the server ‘LauLabNAS1’” — click Continue
  5. In the next pop-up, make sure Registered User is selected
  6. Fill in your NAS username and password, then click Connect
  7. Select the volume you want in the next window; all volumes will be accessible through the LauLabNAS1 connected drive in Finder

Method 2 — via Finder (Connect to Server)

  1. Make sure you are on VPN
  2. Open Finder and press ⌘ + K
  3. In the Connect to Server window, enter:
    • If on VPN: smb://10.18.26.54/<folder>
    • If on VU ethernet: smb://LauLabNAS1/<folder>
  4. Make sure Registered User is selected
  5. Fill in your NAS username and password, then click Connect
  6. Select the desired volume; all volumes will be accessible in Finder

Method 3 — via Finder Network Tab (temporary access on VU ethernet)

  1. Open Finder
  2. In the left sidebar, navigate to Locations → Network
  3. Find LauLabNAS1 among the network drives
  4. Click the Connect As button (top-right of Finder)
  5. A dialog will appear: “You are attempting to connect to the server ‘LauLabNAS1’” — click Continue
  6. Make sure Registered User is selected
  7. Fill in your NAS username and password, then click Connect
  8. All volumes on the NAS will be shown in Finder

Linux

Via NFS

  1. Create an NFS Share on the NAS (Admin only)
    • Log in at http://10.18.26.54:5000/
    • Go to Control Panel → Shared Folder
    • Select the folder you want to share and click Edit
    • Go to the NFS Permissions tab and click Create

    • Fill in the dialog as follows:

      Field Value
      Hostname or IP IP address of the Linux machine (e.g. 10.94.26.35)
      Privilege Read/Write
      Squash No mapping
      Security sys
      Enable asynchronous ✅ Checked
      Allow connections from non-privileged ports ☐ Unchecked
      Allow users to access mounted subfolders ☐ Unchecked
    • Click Save
    • Note the Mount path shown at the bottom of the window (e.g. /volume1/homes) — you will need this for the mount command below

    • ⚠️ Squash setting: currently using “Map all users to admin” on some shares — a safer option is under investigation

  2. Mount on Linux terminal: 
    sudo mount nas_ip:<shared_path> <where_to_mount_path>

  3. [Optional] Permanent mount via /etc/fstab:

    Add the following line to /etc/fstab using vim:

    10.94.27.26:/path_to_share /mnt_path nfs defaults 0 0

    Then run:

    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo mount -a

    ⚠️ Warning: Mount shared folders to different destination directories on your computer. If multiple shared folders are mounted to the same directory, NAS may create random folders unexpectedly.

Via GUI

Use the Synology web interface at http://10.18.26.54:5000/ to manage files through File Station.

Note

Simran will be only using Synology NAS.
entry.summary: how to access and use the lab's Polaris, Rosalind and Synology NAS storage

entry.title: Lau Lab Server Standard Operating Procedure

link.title: Lau Lab Server Standard Operating Procedure

entry.content:
Overview

The Lau lab has two servers, Threadripper and Matisse, each named after the CPU it houses. Both are physically located in Ken’s office, so they depend on the lab’s wired ethernet connection and power supply.

Their main job is processing single-cell RNA-sequencing data, and their hardware was chosen and tuned for that. They handle data that ordinary computers can’t because of memory and time limits. Both are CPU-heavy machines with weak GPUs, so don’t expect to do much GPU-accelerated image analysis or deep learning on them.

  Threadripper Matisse
IP address 10.141.26.164 10.141.26.101
CPU AMD Threadripper 2990WX, 32-core / 64-thread @ 3.00 GHz AMD Ryzen 3900X, 12-core / 24-thread @ 3.8 GHz
GPU AMD FirePro W2100, 2 GB VRAM AMD RX570, 4 GB VRAM
Memory (RAM) 128 GB DDR4 64 GB DDR4
Storage 2 TB SSD, 500 GB SSD, 2× 2 TB HDD 1 TB SSD
OS Ubuntu 20.04 LTS Ubuntu 20.04 LTS

💡 Which server should I use? Matisse has fewer cores and threads, but its base clock is about 26% higher than Threadripper’s. It can’t run as many tasks in parallel, but it runs single-threaded tasks faster. Use Threadripper for large, highly parallel or memory-hungry jobs.

Server Etiquette

Check Usage Before You Start

Every time you connect to a server, check how busy it is with:

top

If someone is running a large job (high CPU and high memory usage), use the #server Slack channel to coordinate resources and timing, or switch to the other server.

Reading the top Output

The top section of the display shows system-level resources. The key fields are:

Field What it means
%Cpu Computational load across all available threads
GiB Mem used RAM used by all connected users. ⚠️ Critical: going over the limit (e.g. 125.8 GB on Threadripper) may automatically kill processes
GiB Swap avail Mem Remaining headroom. The smaller this number, the higher the risk of running out of memory

Useful top Shortcuts

Key Action
E Cycle display units for per-process memory (e.g. bytes → GB)
U Filter processes by username
Shift + E Cycle display units for the system-level summary at the top
Shift + M Sort processes by memory usage
Shift + P Sort processes by CPU usage
q Quit top

Memory Rule of Thumb

⚠️ Do not exceed 30 GB of memory in a single session for standard, count-based scRNA-seq analysis.

30 GB is roughly what you’d use analyzing dozens of combined atlas datasets at once. If your data isn’t that large and you’re near this limit, take a second look at the notebooks you’re running, the datasets loaded into those environments and the variables you’re holding in memory.

If you’ve determined you truly need more than 30 GB and other users are connected to your server, post an advisory message in #server on Slack so others know. Failing to do so will earn you sad emojis 😢 and may push us toward automated resource restrictions, which limit everyone.

Connection and Environment Setup

Using the servers requires setup on your local machine (home desktop, laptop, lab desktop, etc.) and on your server profile. Once that’s done, you can connect and set up your analysis environment.

1. Connect from Your Local Machine

  1. Connect to the Vanderbilt VPN using Pulse Secure (only needed off-campus)
  2. Open a terminal:
    • Windows: install Git Bash and open it
    • Mac / Linux: open the built-in Terminal

  3. Run the SSH command for your server:

    Threadripper

    ssh -L 1234:127.0.0.1:XXXX your-username@10.141.26.164

    Matisse

    ssh -L 1234:127.0.0.1:XXXX your-username@10.141.26.101
    • XXXX is a 4-digit port number above 9000 of your choosing. It’s the port the server uses to send data back to your machine, so remember it for later.
    • This command connects to the server and forwards that port to port 1234 on your local machine.
  4. Enter your password when prompted. By default it’s the server name followed by your first and last initials, all lowercase (e.g. threadripperab). Change it after your first login with passwd.

💡 Tip: Save the SSH command in a text file (e.g. connect.sh) and run it with bash connect.sh so you don’t have to retype it every time.

2. Use tmux (Highly Recommended)

A dropped connection usually terminates everything you were running. tmux creates sessions you can detach from and re-attach to, so your work survives disconnects.

Action Command
Start a new session tmux new -s scanpy_session (a green bar at the bottom means it worked)
Detach (send to background) Ctrl + b, release, then d
Re-attach tmux attach-session -t scanpy_session
List running sessions tmux ls
Close a session completely exit (while attached)

Use ls at any time to see the files in your current directory.

3. Install Anaconda

  1. Download the installer: 
    curl -O https://repo.anaconda.com/archive/Anaconda3-2020.02-Linux-x86_64.sh
  2. Run it: 
    bash Anaconda3-2020.02-Linux-x86_64.sh
  3. Respond to the prompts:
    • Accept the license terms
    • Keep the default install location
    • Say yes to initializing conda / modifying your bash profile
  4. Disconnect (exit) and reconnect to the server. If everything worked, you’ll see (base) at the left of your command prompt.

4. Create a Conda Environment

Environments keep each project’s Python packages separate, since different packages may need conflicting dependency versions.

  1. Create an environment (answer yes to any prompts): 
    conda create --name my_env python=3.7
  2. Activate it: 
    conda activate my_env
  3. Make sure the environment is active before installing anything. Packages installed with pip install or conda install are available only while that environment is active.
  4. Install JupyterLab: 
    pip install jupyterlab

5. Launch JupyterLab on the Server

jupyter lab --no-browser --port=XXXX

⚠️ XXXX must be the same port number you used in your SSH command.

This hosts JupyterLab on the server at that port, which is forwarded to your local machine.

Managing the Jupyter Process

Action Command
Suspend the process and get your terminal back Ctrl + Z
Resume it in the background (keeps Jupyter running while you use the terminal) bg
List background jobs jobs
Bring it back to the foreground fg
Stop Jupyter (while in the foreground) Ctrl + C twice

⚠️ After Ctrl + Z, Jupyter is paused until you run bg or fg. Your browser tab will hang until you do.

6. Open Jupyter in Your Local Browser

  1. In any browser on your local machine, go to: localhost:1234
  2. The first time, it will ask for a token. In your server terminal, find the output line that looks like localhost:XXXX/?token=..., then copy everything after token= into the browser. Make sure you don’t copy any extra spaces.
  3. You should now see your JupyterLab environment, hosted on the server.

💡 All file paths in Jupyter are relative to the server directory where you ran jupyter lab.

Exiting Server Operations

On your local machine:

  1. Save everything (Ctrl + S works as usual)
  2. Go to the Running tab in JupyterLab and shut down active notebooks

On the server terminal:

  1. Make sure the Jupyter process is in the foreground. Use fg if needed. (If you can’t type commands, it’s already in the foreground.)
  2. Press Ctrl + C once to bring up the exit prompt, then again to confirm
  3. Type exit to disconnect. You can now close the window.

Resetting Everything

If things get stuck and you need to start over, or you’re completely done with the server:

pkill -u your-username

⚠️ Warning: This kills all processes running under your username. Anything not saved to disk will be lost.

Copying Files Between Servers

Log in to the destination server first, then pull files from the other one.

Logged in to Matisse, copying from Threadripper:

scp username@10.141.26.164:/home/username/* /home/username

Logged in to Threadripper, copying from Matisse:

scp username@10.141.26.101:/home/username/* /home/username

To copy whole directories, add the -r flag:

scp -r username@10.141.26.164:/home/username/my_folder /home/username
entry.summary: how to connect to and responsibly use the lab's Threadripper and Matisse analysis servers

entry.title: a post with marimo snippets
entry.content:
marimo notebooks can run Python directly in the reader’s browser. Opt a page in from its front matter:

---
layout: post
title: a post with marimo snippets
marimo: true
---

Nothing is loaded on pages without that flag, so bundling the plugin costs nothing site-wide.

Runnable snippets

Wrap fenced Python blocks in a container and the runtime turns them into an interactive notebook after the page loads:

import marimo as mo

slider = mo.ui.slider(1, 20, value=5, label="n")
slider

mo.md(f"The first {slider.value} squares: {[i**2 for i in range(1, slider.value + 1)]}")

Until the runtime has moved those blocks into place the container stays hidden, so readers never see the raw source flash before it becomes a notebook.

Embedding a hosted notebook

If you already publish a notebook — on marimo.app or your own WASM host — embed it instead:

{% al_marimo_embed src="https://marimo.app/l/your-notebook" height="700px" caption="Sampling demo" %}

The frame is sandboxed without allow-same-origin, so the embedded notebook cannot reach this page’s storage or cookies.

A note on what this loads

The marimo-snippets runtime is vendored into the plugin at a pinned version and served from your own site, rather than pulled from a CDN — so no third-party origin executes script in your readers’ pages. Running a notebook does contact marimo’s host, which is worth knowing before you opt a page in.

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. Done. Just one step more. Check your inbox to confirm your subscription.

You can also subscribe with a different email address.
  
        Your information will be used in accordance with Google's privacy policy. You may opt out at any time.
entry.summary: We’re sharing updates across our Gemini family of models and a glimpse of Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants.

}

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
```

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}

\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
